engage.heading: The amazing elasticity of tendons
engage.text:
The energy used in an animal’s motion arises mostly from the muscular force generated to support the animal’s weight and the work associated with moving the animal’s centre of mass and body segments. When moving at high speeds, animals use bouncy gaits to conserve muscle work. At these higher speeds, the energy saving is mainly achieved by the storage and recovery of elastic potential energy in tendons and ligaments. Tendons are connective tissue mainly composed of collagen fibres that attach muscle to bone.
Tendons are remarkably efficient. Testing in human runners has found that the mechanical energy that our tendons return to us is very similar to other mammals and running birds, 5–13%. The mechanical energy is the energy from the muscular forces that generate and maintain movement. The exception to this is wallabies and kangaroos, which are more than twice as mechanically efficient as humans.
Wallabies and kangaroos have unusually long tendons that have the ability to store larger amounts of elastic potential energy. This allows kangaroos to hop at high speeds while using very little energy.

chunks.heading: Elasticity
chunks.text: When an object compresses, extends or twists and then returns to its original shape, the material has stored energy by changing shape. Any material that can change shape and then return to its original shape is called an elastic material. All elastic materials have an elastic limit, this is the maximum stress that a material can be placed under without causing permanent deformation. Many solid materials are elastic, such as rubber, neoprene and steel. Materials that change shape permanently when deformed only slightly are referred to as plastic materials. Mud clay and plasticine are all examples of plastic materials.

chunks.heading: Hooke’s law
chunks.text:
Springs are used extensively in a range of machines and devices. Toys, pens, electronics, mattresses, medical devices, automatic watches, mining and drilling equipment and vehicles are just a few examples of where springs are used.
We have been able to utilise springs so effectively because we have known about their properties for over 300 years. In 1676 British physicist Robert Hooke first proposed Hooke’s law, that in an ideal spring, the force applied to the spring is directly proportional to its extension or compression. Imagine a specific spring resting horizontally – when no force is applied to the spring there will be no extension in the spring. When 50 N of force is applied to this specific spring, it extends by 0.2 m; when 100 N of force is applied to the spring it extends by 0.4 m. A force–extension graph of the spring is shown in the figure above.
The constant linear relationship between the force applied and the extension highlights Hooke’s law, that force is directly proportional to extension. The gradient of this graph is known as the spring constant, k, and as you are dividing newtons by metres the unit for the spring constant is N m$^{-1}$. The gradient, and therefore the spring constant for the spring, in the graph above can be calculated as follows:
$\text{gradient} = k = \frac{\text{rise}}{\text{run}} = \frac{200 - 0}{0.8 - 0} = 250\ \text{N m}^{-1}$
The spring constant gives an indication of the stiffness of the spring; the higher the spring constant, the more force is required to extend or compress the spring and therefore the stiffer it is. For example, a spring that has a spring constant of 500 N m$^{-1}$ would take twice as much force to extend it an equal amount as the spring with a spring constant of 250 N m$^{-1}$. This is shown in the graphs below.
Hooke’s law can be represented mathematically as follows:
$F = -kx$
There is a negative sign to indicate that the spring’s restoring force acts in the opposite direction to the compression or extension. For simplicity, this book will omit the negative sign from this point onwards. This means that the formula will indicate the magnitude of the force on the spring and hence the magnitude of the force by the spring. While the above equation only refers to springs, the relationship holds true for all solid elastic materials.

chunks.heading: Elastic potential energy
chunks.text:
When an elastic material is compressed, extended or twisted, it stores energy. This stored energy is known as elastic potential energy or elastic potential energy. When the elastic potential energy is released, the object will return to its original shape. Imagine a spring that has a spring constant, k. A force–compression graph of the spring is shown on the right.
You should note that the values shown on the y-axis are a measure of force and values on the x-axis are a measure of distance (compression or extension). This means that this graph is just a special force–distance graph, and the area under a force–distance graph is work. This means that the area under a force–compression/extension graph is the work done to compress or extend the objects as well as the amount of elastic potential energy stored in the object. For the force–compression graph above, the elastic potential energy would be given by the area under the triangle; therefore:
$\text{elastic potential energy} = E_{\text{s}} = \frac{1}{2}(F)(x)$
Hooke’s law states that F = kx. Therefore, the force, F, in the above equation can be substituted for kx as shown:
$E_{\text{s}} = \frac{1}{2}(k)(x)(x)$
$E_{\text{s}} = \frac{1}{2}kx^{2}$

chunks.heading: Elastic potential energy increases with extension
chunks.text:
When trying to extend a spring, it gets harder to change the shape of the spring the more you extend it. To extend a spring by 1 cm when it is resting does not take as much energy as extending the same spring by 1 cm when it is already stretched. This is because the more you stretch a spring, the greater the restoring force becomes and therefore more energy must be applied to overcome this force. This is also true when trying to compress a spring. This is shown graphically in Figure 9C–7, with a spring that has a spring constant of 200 N m$^{-1}$.
As the spring extends, it takes more and more energy to extend it by the same amount. The energy required to extend the spring by 1 cm is represented by the shaded region in the graph. It is clear that the longer the spring becomes, the more energy is required to extend the spring by 1 cm.
Therefore, when finding the change in elastic potential energy, you can either find the area under the graph or take away the elastic potential energy of the initial length, $x_{\text{i}}$, from the elastic potential energy of the final length, $x_{\text{f}}$:
$\Delta E_{\text{s}} = \frac{1}{2}kx_{\text{f}}^{2} - \frac{1}{2}kx_{\text{i}}^{2}$

chunks.heading: Energy transformations in a horizontal spring system
chunks.text:
Imagine an ideal spring that works the same in compression and extension. The spring is lying horizontally on a frictionless surface, with one end fixed against a wall and the other end attached to a free object. If the object is pulled back and let go, it will oscillate about an equilibrium position. When the object is at the equilibrium position, it will have no net force on it. The object will have no net force on it because the spring is at its natural length, it is not compressed or extended, and the force due to gravity of the object is balanced by the normal force applied by the surface on the object.
As the spring oscillates, the kinetic energy and elastic potential energy will fluctuate between maximum values and zero. Since the total energy, $E_{\text{T}}$, will remain the same throughout the oscillation the sum of the kinetic energy, $E_{\text{k}}$, and elastic potential energy, $E_{\text{s}}$, at any given point will be equal to the total energy. This can been represented by the following formula:
$E_{\text{T}} = E_{\text{k}} + E_{\text{s}}$
$E_{\text{T}} = \frac{1}{2}mv^{2} + \frac{1}{2}kx^{2}$
Position 1: At position 1 the spring is fully extended, it is a point of maximum spring potential energy and zero kinetic energy. As the object moves towards the equilibrium position (2) the kinetic energy increases and the spring potential energy decreases.
Position 2: At the equilibrium positions (2 and 4) the spring will have maximum kinetic energy and zero spring potential energy. Once the object passes the equilibrium position the spring begins to compress, slowing the object down. The kinetic energy will decrease while the spring potential energy increases.
Position 3: At position 3 the spring potential energy will be a maximum and the kinetic energy will be zero. The object will then gain kinetic energy and lose spring potential energy as it moves back to the equilibrium (4).
Position 4: At the equilibrium position again the spring will have maximum kinetic energy and zero spring potential energy. Once past the equilibrium the kinetic energy of the object will decrease and the spring potential energy will increase.
Position 1: This decrease in kinetic energy will continue until the spring comes momentarily to rest at position 1, ready to repeat the cycle.

chunks.heading: Energy transformations in a vertical spring system
chunks.text:
For a vertical spring system, imagine an ideal spring with one end fixed to a ceiling and the other end attached to an object that is free to move. If the object is dropped and allowed to move freely under the influence of gravity, it will oscillate about an equilibrium position. When the object attached to a vertical spring is at the equilibrium position, it will have no forces on it. This is because the upwards spring force will balance the downwards force due to gravity.
The upwards spring force balancing the downwards force due to gravity is shown mathematically below:
$kx = mg$
The equilibrium position is the position of maximum kinetic energy. As the spring oscillates about the equilibrium position, the gravitational potential energy, elastic potential energy and kinetic energy will fluctuate between maximum values and zero.
Before analysing the motion of a vertical spring system you must define the point of zero gravitational potential energy. It will be the lowest point of the spring’s oscillation (position 3 in the diagram).
When the object is initially dropped (position 1), the spring is in its natural position, under no compression or extension. This means that the spring potential energy and kinetic energy are both equal to zero, while the gravitational potential energy is at a maximum. As the object is pulled down by the force of gravity its spring potential energy and kinetic energy increase, while the gravitational potential energy decreases. At the equilibrium positions (2 and 4), the kinetic energy is a maximum. Between positions 2 and 3, the object passes the equilibrium position, the kinetic energy starts to decrease, the gravitational potential energy continues to decrease, and the spring potential energy continues to increase. At position 3 the kinetic energy and gravitational potential energy are both equal to zero, while the spring potential energy is at a maximum. Between positions 3 and 4, the object then moves upwards, increasing both the kinetic energy and gravitational potential energy, while decreasing the spring potential energy. At position 4, the object passes the equilibrium position, the kinetic energy starts to decrease, the gravitational potential energy continues to increase, and the spring potential energy continues to decrease, until the object returns to position 1 and the cycle repeats.

chunks.heading: Mathematical relationships in a vertical spring system
chunks.text:
The gravitational potential energy lost by the object will be transformed into the elastic potential energy and kinetic energy of the system. This relationship can be represented by the formula:
$E_{\text{g}} = E_{\text{s}} + E_{\text{k}}$
$mg\Delta h = \frac{1}{2}kx^{2} + \frac{1}{2}mv^{2}$
Since the change in height is equal to the change in length of the spring, Δh can be replaced with an x as shown below:
$mgx = \frac{1}{2}kx^{2} + \frac{1}{2}mv^{2}$

A group of students is conducting an experiment with an ideal spring that has a spring constant, k, of 21.8 N m$^{-1}$. The spring has an unstretched length of 30 cm. The students attach a mass of 300 g to the bottom of the spring and allow it to oscillate freely when it is released. When the spring is released, the spring has a maximum extension of x cm. The situation is shown to the right.
a Find the extension of the spring at its lowest point of oscillation. You can ignore the mass of the spring itself and frictional losses.
b When is the speed of the mass on the spring a maximum? Explain your answer.
c Calculate the extension of the spring when the velocity is a maximum.
d Calculate the maximum velocity of the spring throughout its oscillation.
checkins.answer:
a $mg\Delta h = \frac{1}{2}k\Delta x^{2}$, since $\Delta h = x$
$mg = \frac{1}{2}kx$
$x = \frac{2mg}{k} = \frac{(2)(0.3)(9.8)}{21.8} = 0.270\ \text{m}$
b The velocity is a maximum when the gravity force on the mass is balanced by the spring force. This is because the acceleration on the mass up until this point is in the same direction but decreasing. The mass will continue to accelerate until it reaches this point, where the forces are balanced, and after this point the net force and therefore the acceleration will be in the opposite direction to the direction of the velocity.
c $kx = mg$
$x = \frac{mg}{k} = \frac{(0.3)(9.8)}{21.8} = 0.135\ \text{m}$
d The energy at the release point will equal the energy at the equilibrium position (fastest point).
$\Delta E_{\text{g}} = E_{\text{s}} + E_{\text{k}}$
$mgx = \frac{1}{2}kx^{2} + \frac{1}{2}mv^{2}$
$v = \sqrt{\frac{2}{m}\left(mgx - \frac{1}{2}kx^{2}\right)} = \sqrt{\frac{2}{0.3}\left((0.3)(9.8)(0.135) - \frac{1}{2}(21.8)(0.135)^{2}\right)} = 1.15\ \text{m s}^{-1}$

A spring with a natural (unextended length) of 10 cm is hung vertically and a mass of 4 kg is attached to the spring, which causes it to oscillate. At the lowest point of its oscillation, the spring has a total length of 16 cm. A diagram of this situation is shown below.
a What is the length of the spring when the velocity is a maximum? Explain why this length corresponds to the maximum velocity.
b Calculate the spring constant of the spring.
c As the spring extends from 10 cm to 16 cm in length, describe the changes that occur in the gravitational potential energy of the mass and the elastic potential energy.
d What is the maximum velocity of the mass throughout the oscillation?
section_questions.answer:
a The total length of the spring would be 13 cm. At this point the spring force and weight force are equal; this is called the equilibrium position. The spring will accelerate towards the equilibrium position. Therefore, the moment the mass moved to the equilibrium position it must be at its maximum velocity as in the next moment the mass will move past the equilibrium position. This means the direction of acceleration will change, causing the spring to decelerate.
b When the spring is half of its maximum extension, the weight force and the spring force on the mass are equal, therefore:
$mg = kx$
$k = \frac{mg}{x} = \frac{(4)(9.8)}{(0.03)} = 1.31\times10^{3}\ \text{N m}^{-1}$
c When the spring has a length of 10 cm, it has maximum gravitational potential energy. The mass then falls, converting its gravitational potential energy to spring potential energy. When the spring is 16 cm in length, all of the gravitational potential energy of the mass has been converted into spring potential energy.
d Take $E_{\text{g}} = 0$ at the equilibrium position, where the velocity will be a maximum.
$E_{\text{total}}$ (release point) = $E_{\text{total}}$ (equilibrium)
$E_{\text{g}} = E_{\text{s}} + E_{\text{k}}$
$mgx = \frac{1}{2}kx^{2} + \frac{1}{2}mv^{2}$
$v = \sqrt{\frac{2}{m}\left(mgx - \frac{1}{2}kx^{2}\right)} = \sqrt{\frac{2}{4}\left((4)(9.8)(0.03) - \frac{1}{2}(1.31\times10^{3})(0.03)^{2}\right)} = 0.542\ \text{m s}^{-1}$

A pinball machine uses a handle, spring and soft plunger in a cylinder to launch a ball into the machine. In the figure below, the top diagram shows the system in the rest position. In the lower diagram, a hand pulls back on the handle compressing the spring. The ball rolls back against the plunger due to the cylinder sloping very slightly downwards towards the handle end (ignore any gravitational effects).
A force–length of the spring graph is shown below.
a What is the resting length of the spring?
b What is the spring constant for this spring?
c Calculate the work done to compress the spring from 0.14 m to 0.02 m.
d If the ball has a mass of 0.35 kg and the spring is compressed by 0.12 m, calculate the speed of the ball when the spring is released.
section_questions.answer:
a 0.140 m; the resting length is when the force on the spring is zero.
b Because this graph is a force–distance graph, the absolute value of the gradient will give the spring constant.
$k = \text{gradient} = \left|\frac{36-0}{0.02-0.14}\right| = 300\ \text{N m}^{-1}$
c Because this graph is a force–distance graph, this can also be done by finding the area under the graph.
$E_{\text{s}} = \frac{1}{2}kx^{2} = \frac{1}{2}(300)(0.12)^{2} = 2.16\ \text{J}$
d $E_{\text{s}} = E_{\text{k}}$
$\frac{1}{2}mv^{2} = \frac{1}{2}kx^{2}$
$v = \sqrt{\frac{kx^{2}}{m}} = \sqrt{\frac{(300)(0.12)^{2}}{(0.35)}} = 3.51\ \text{m s}^{-1}$

section_questions.question:
A mass of 2.0 kg is suspended from a spring, with spring constant k = 50 N m$^{-1}$, as shown in the diagram below. It is released from the unstretched position of the spring and falls a distance of 0.80 m. Take the zero of gravitational potential energy at its lowest point and the gravitational field strength as 10 N kg$^{-1}$.
a Calculate the change in gravitational potential energy as the mass moves from the top position to the lowest position.
b Calculate the spring potential energy at its lowest point.
c Calculate the speed of the mass at its midpoint (maximum speed).
© VCAA, 2015
section_questions.answer:
a $\Delta E_{\text{g}} = mg\Delta h = (2)(10)(0.8) = 16\ \text{J}$
b $E_{\text{s}} = \frac{1}{2}kx^{2} = \frac{1}{2}(50)(0.8)^{2} = 16\ \text{J}$
c $E_{\text{total}} = E_{\text{g}} + E_{\text{s}} + E_{\text{k}} = E_{\text{g}} + E_{\text{s}} + \frac{1}{2}mv^{2}$
$v = \sqrt{\frac{2(E_{\text{total}} - E_{\text{g}} - E_{\text{s}})}{m}} = \sqrt{\frac{2(16-8-4)}{(2)}} = 2\ \text{m s}^{-1}$

section_questions.question:
A toaster manufacturer is testing springs for their latest toaster. In their design, a single spring is used in the toaster to pop a 38-gram piece of toast back up, once it has finished cooking. The engineers make and test two new springs. They test them by adding masses to springs and measuring how much the spring compress due to the masses. The measurements are taken with a ruler that has markings every millimetre. A diagram of this situation is shown below.
The results of their tests are shown in the table below (note that you can take gravity to be 10 N kg$^{-1}$ in this experiment).
| Spring 1 Compression (mm) | Mass (g) | Force (N) | Spring 2 Compression (mm) | Mass (g) | Force (N) |
| 1.4 | 10 | | 6.7 | 10 | |
| 2.9 | 20 | | 13.3 | 20 | |
| 4.3 | 30 | | 20.1 | 30 | |
| 5.7 | 40 | | 26.6 | 40 | |
a Copy the table and complete the force columns of the engineer’s results.
b Use the information provided in the table to graph the results on the set of axes provided below. Your graph should include an accurate scale, a line of best fit and error bars for the x-axis only.
c List the independent and dependent variables.
d Use the line of best fit from your graph to determine the spring constant of spring 1 and spring 2.
e The engineers must consider how high the 38-gram piece of toast will be launched out of the toaster. In order to do this, the engineers use the following equation to predict the height that the toast will achieve:
$h = \frac{k\Delta x^{2}}{2mg}$
Show how the engineers derived this equation.
f In the toaster, the spring will be compressed by 5 cm. Will spring 1 or spring 2 be most appropriate to use in the toaster? Use at least two calculations to justify your response.
g An engineer points out after the testing that there was a systematic error in their experiment. The engineer says that when the spring is placed vertically, it will be slightly compressed due to its own weight force. Comment on how this systematic error would affect the predicted value for the spring constant.
section_questions.answer:
a Spring 1 & 2: Mass (g) 10, 20, 30, 40 → Force (N) 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4
b (graph: see img/9C_SQ10b_answer.jpg)
c Independent: the mass applied to compress the springs; dependent: the compression of the spring
d Spring 1 ≈ 70 N m$^{-1}$
Spring 2 ≈ 15 N m$^{-1}$
$\text{Gradient} = k = \frac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1}$
e $\frac{1}{2}k\Delta x^{2} = mgh$ rearranges to $h = \frac{kx^{2}}{2mg}$
f Students should use the formula $h = \frac{kx^{2}}{2mg}$ to determine the height that the toast reaches when the spring is released, the spring constant, k, should be the constant calculated in part d. For example:
$h_1 = \frac{(70)(0.05)^{2}}{2(0.038)(10)} = 0.23\ \text{m}$
$h_2 = \frac{(15)(0.05)^{2}}{2(0.038)(10)} = 0.049\ \text{m}$
The most appropriate spring is spring 2, as it will launch the toast about 5 cm in the air. If spring 1 was used, the toast would be launched more than 20 cm into the air.
g The true values of the compression for the given force applied to the spring would be consistently higher than expected, as the additional force from the springs own mass was not accounted for. This means since $k = \frac{F}{x}$, the force is lower and the compression is higher, which means the predicted spring would be lower than the true spring constant.

questions.question: When clicking a spring-loaded pen, a force of 6.5 N is applied to compress the spring 11 mm. Calculate the spring constant of the spring.

A group of engineers are testing two springs, Spring A and Spring B, for use in a pinball machine. The engineers decide that they want to go with the stiffer of the two springs to save on material cost because a smaller spring can be used in the machines. The results of their tests are displayed on the force–compression graph below.
a Which spring, A or B, will the engineers select? Give a reason for your answer.
questions.answer:
Spring A (1 mark)
Spring A has a steeper gradient and is therefore stiffer. (1 mark)

questions.question: Calculate the spring constant of Spring A.
Calculate the amount of elastic potential energy stored in Spring B when it is compressed by 100 mm.
By how much would Spring A need to be compressed to contain the same amount of elastic potential energy as Spring B when it is compressed by 100 mm?

A 55 cm spring, with a spring constant of 4500 N m$^{-1}$, is initially compressed down to 45 cm and is then released back to a length of 53 cm. Calculate the amount of energy released when the spring was released back to a length of 53 cm.
questions.answer:
$\Delta E_{s} = \frac{1}{2}kx_{f}^{2} - \frac{1}{2}kx_{i}^{2} = \frac{1}{2}(4500)(0.02)^{2} - \frac{1}{2}(4500)(0.1)^{2} = -21.6\ \text{J}$
Note that there is a negative sign in front of the energy because the energy is being given out.

questions.question:
A spring, with a spring constant of 250 N m$^{-1}$, is fixed to a wall at one end and at the other end is it attached to a 1.5 kg mass. The mass is free to move on the frictionless surface that it is resting on. A person extends the spring by 20 cm and then allows it to oscillate freely. The spring works the same in compression and in extension. A diagram of this situation is shown below.
a Calculate the total energy in the system.
questions.answer:
The total energy will be the energy when the spring is fully extended, therefore:
$E_{s} = \frac{1}{2}kx^{2} = \frac{1}{2}(250)(0.2^{2}) = 5\ \text{J}$

questions.question: Describe the energy transformations that occur when the spring is released from a position of 20 cm of extension and moves to a position of full compression.
questions.answer:
Once the spring is released from its fully extended position, the elastic potential energy will transform into kinetic energy until it reaches the equilibrium position. (1 mark)
Once the mass passes the equilibrium position, the kinetic energy begins to convert into elastic potential energy until the spring is fully compressed. (1 mark)

questions.question: When will the maximum velocity of the mass occur? Justify your answer.
questions.answer:
The velocity will be at a maximum at the equilibrium point, when the spring is at its natural length. (1 mark)
This means that there is no net force on the mass, so the acceleration of the mass is zero. (1 mark)
Therefore, before this point, the mass would have been accelerating in the direction of travel and after this point the mass will begin to decelerate. (1 mark)

questions.question: Calculate the maximum velocity of the mass.
questions.answer:
$E_{T} = \frac{1}{2}mv^{2} + \frac{1}{2}kx^{2}$
The velocity is at a maximum when there is no extension in the spring, therefore: (1 mark)
$v = \sqrt{\frac{2E_{T}}{m}} = \sqrt{\frac{(2)(5)}{1.5}}$ (1 mark)
$= 2.58\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ (1 mark)

questions.question:
A spring, with a spring constant of 150 N m$^{-1}$, is hung vertically from a ceiling. A 5 kg mass is attached to the base of the spring and the spring is allowed to oscillate freely. For this question, ignore the effects of air resistance and friction and assume that the spring’s mass is negligible.
a When is the velocity of the mass at a maximum? Justify your answer.
questions.answer:
The velocity will be at a maximum at the equilibrium point, when the spring force is balanced by the force due to gravity. (1 mark)
At this point, the forces on the mass are balanced and the acceleration is zero. (1 mark)
Therefore, before this point, the mass would have been accelerating in the direction of travel and after this point the mass will begin to decelerate. (1 mark)

questions.question: What is the extension of the spring when the velocity of the mass is a maximum?
When the mass has fallen 3 cm from its highest point, what is the velocity of the spring?

skills.heading: How to ‘explain’ your answer
skills.text:
Exams will commonly ask you to ‘explain’ your answer. To explain means to present accurate and concise evidence that supports your answer. Consider the following question.
Question
A mass, that is attached to an ideal spring, is dropped and allowed to oscillate freely in the vertical direction. When is the velocity of the mass at a maximum? Explain your answer. (3 marks)
Solution
• The velocity will be at a maximum at the equilibrium point, when the spring force is balanced by the force due to gravity. (1 mark)
• When the forces on the mass are balanced, the acceleration is zero. (1 mark)
• Therefore, before this point the mass would have been accelerating in the direction of travel and after this point the mass will begin to decelerate. (1 mark)
The answer is set out in three dot points; each dot point makes a distinct point and would be awarded one mark. When answering ‘explain’ questions, you should look at the number of marks and use that as a guide of how many points to make. Make sure that you are answering the question presented and not just writing a pre-prepared answer that is not specific to the question. Answers should be clear and concise. Remember that you will not be marked down for using dot points, in fact they can help you structure your answer.
